bib.title: A Survey on Post-training of Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "A Survey on Post-Training of Large Language Models" (PoLMs), Guiyao Tie et al. (15 authors, HUST/Lehigh/etc.), arXiv:2503.06072v3, 1 Aug 2025 (preprint; "Latest Update: Mar., 2025").

COVERAGE: Read all 87 pages. Extraction was 333,168 chars; I read chars 0-216,000 in full (body, sections 1-11). Chars ~216,000-333,168 are the reference list. I skimmed it only to resolve citations and found no appendix. Extraction was clean text, but some equations are flattened, and the first dump hit a surrogate-character encoding error that I worked around by re-encoding. No page was skipped for being unreadable.

NOTE FOR THE TARGET NOTE (01-rl-foundations): this is a breadth survey. It has NO experiments and NO new results. Almost everything is descriptive, with no benchmark numbers for RL methods. The few numbers are citation-level. Its value for the note is (a) the notation chain (advantage, PPO clip, KL-regularized reward, DPO, GRPO, MDP-for-reasoning) and (b) a taxonomy. Several of its DeepSeek-R1 details look unreliable (see LIMITS).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Advantage is Q minus V, and the PPO objective clips the probability ratio to a trust band.
  number: A = Q - V (Eq 1); clip(r_t, 1-eps, 1+eps) (Eq 2)
  setup: standard PPO as the survey presents it for RLHF. The value function is fit by MSE to the realized return (Eq 3).
  quote: "The advantage function Aπ(s, a) measures how advantageous it is to take action a in state s under the current policy π, compared to the expected value of actions in that state. It is formally defined as the difference between the action-value function Qπ(s, a) and the state-value function V π(s)"
  where: p.10 (offset ~54,000-56,000)
- claim: GRPO is a PPO variant that drops the critic and estimates the baseline from a group of sampled outputs. Its objective is PPO's clipped ratio, averaged per token and per output, plus a beta-weighted KL to the reference.
  number: Eq 8; group {o_1..o_G}, hyperparameters eps and beta
  setup: introduced in DeepSeekMath [64]; the survey does not give the advantage formula and defers it to "subsection 5.2", which never states it.
  quote: "GRPO omits the critic model, instead estimating the baseline using group scores, which significantly reduces training resource consumption compared to PPO."
  where: pp.11-12
- claim: The RLHF objective is expected reward under the policy. In the practical version, the reward is penalised by beta times the log-ratio against the original model, which keeps the policy near the pretrained one.
  number: Eq 5, Eq 13
  setup: GPT-2 summarisation cited as the example (CNN/DailyMail, TL;DR).
  quote: "To discourage the policy π from straying too far from the initial model ρ, a penalty term controlled by the hyperparameter β is introduced into the reward function"
  where: p.20
- claim: The DPO derivation runs in five steps. The KL-regularised optimum is a Boltzmann reweighting of pi_ref. Inverting it gives the reward as beta times the log-ratio plus beta log Z(x). Z(x) cancels in Bradley-Terry pairwise comparisons. This yields a logistic loss on beta-scaled log-ratio differences, with no explicit reward model.
  number: Eqs 14-20
  setup: preference triplets (x, y_w, y_l); pi_ref is typically the SFT model and stays frozen.
  quote: "where β log Z(x) is a constant that does not affect pairwise comparisons of rewards. If the optimal policy π∗ is known, the true reward r∗(x, y) can be determined up to this constant."
  where: p.23
- claim: Reasoning can be cast as an MDP. The state is the query plus the prior reasoning steps. The action is the next token or reasoning step. Transitions are mostly deterministic (autoregressive). The reward is either sparse (final answer) or dense (step-wise). The objective is the discounted return.
  number: J(theta) = E[sum_{t=1..T} gamma^t R(s_t,a_t)] (Eq 21)
  setup: the survey's own formulation. It names PPO or A2C as the solvers.
  quote: "reasoning transitions in LLMs are predominantly deterministic, driven by the model's autoregressive outputs or structured inference rules"
  where: pp.28-29
- claim: Reasoning reward designs come in four kinds. Binary correctness is simple but high-variance. Step-wise accuracy rewards are denser. Self-consistency rewards score agreement across sampled paths. Preference-based rewards come from RLHF or RLAIF.
  number: r_T = 1 if correct, else 0
  setup: general taxonomy, no empirical comparison.
  quote: "binary correctness rewards, assigning rT = 1 for a correct final answer and rT = 0 otherwise, which is simple but introduces high variance due to sparse feedback"
  where: p.29
- claim: DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained with GRPO and pure RL from the base model with no SFT. DeepSeek-R1 adds a cold-start long-CoT SFT stage. The survey's Fig 13 shows a rule-based reward system, a language-consistency reward, and a second RL stage for helpfulness and harmlessness.
  number: none for training; the distillation corpus is about 800k = 200k + 600k
  setup: DeepSeek-V3-Base. This is descriptive and the survey reports no benchmark scores.
  quote: "The DeepSeek-R1-Zero model leverages a sophisticated variant of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), termed Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)"
  where: p.29-30, Fig 13
- claim: R1 distillation is plain SFT of smaller Qwen and LLaMA models on teacher outputs.
  number: ~800k samples (200k non-reasoning from DeepSeek-V3, 600k reasoning from R1-Stage1)
  setup: SFT only, no RL on the students.
  quote: "a curated dataset of approximately 800k samples generated by a large teacher model, comprising 200k non-reasoning instances derived from DeepSeek-V3 and 600k reasoned instances produced by the DeepSeek-R1-Stage1 checkpoint"
  where: p.38
- claim: RLAIF is reported as comparable to RLHF.
  number: none
  setup: second-hand, citing [157] (Lee et al., "RLAIF vs. RLHF", ICML), judged by human raters.
  quote: "RLAIF can achieve performance comparable to or even superior to RLHF, as evaluated by human raters. Notably, RLAIF not only surpasses traditional supervised fine-tuning baselines but does so with an LLM preference labeler of the same scale as the policy model"
  where: p.21
- claim: ReFT is SFT warm-up followed by PPO on sampled CoTs. Correct answers get positive reward and wrong ones get negative reward. No extra training data is used.
  number: none
  setup: cited from [103] (Luong et al. 2024). The survey gives no figures.
  quote: "ReFT achieves these improvements without requiring additional or augmented training data, learning solely from the existing dataset used during the SFT phase."
  where: p.17
- claim: RLOO is REINFORCE without a value model. It treats the whole response as one action and learns from a sparse reward.
  number: none
  setup: described as a DPO-variant-adjacent method.
  quote: "RLOO [112] leverages the REINFORCE algorithm without training a value model, substantially reducing computational overhead. It treats the entire response as a single action and learns from sparse rewards"
  where: p.24
- claim: Timeline of RLHF. The survey dates RLHF to 2021 [45], PPO adoption to 2022, ChatGPT to late 2022, and DPO to 2023.
  number: 2021 / 2022 / 2023
  setup: the survey's own dating, which is loose. Ref [45] is InstructGPT, which is dated Mar-2022 in Table 1 and Table 2.
  quote: "advent of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) in 2021 [45]"
  where: p.8
- claim: Table 2 gives a comparison grid of alignment methods. Axes include explicit vs implicit reward model, point vs preference, response vs token level, on- vs off-policy, and online vs offline. It lists InstructGPT, Anthropic RLHF, DPO, RRHF, PRO, RLOO, GRPO, SimPO, and others.
  number: none (categorical)
  setup: 2022-2024 methods
  quote: "GRPO [114] Implicit Point Response Positive AI Reference Off Online Feb-2024"
  where: p.18, Table 2

LIMITS
- No new experiments. Survey only. The authors' own stated gaps (Section 10) are: binary reward signals and heavy human feedback "inability to generalize effectively across complex, open-ended tasks"; RL is resource-intensive, since DeepSeek-R1's approach "requir[es] extensive computational infrastructure"; "PEFT ... performance often degrades on large-scale datasets"; ethical-alignment bias risk; and context-dependent trust. These are asserted, not measured.
- The survey is thin on pedagogy. The GRPO advantage formula (group-normalised reward) is never written out, and PPO's KL penalty vs clip is not distinguished.
- Likely errors, to treat with caution and not cite as fact:
  1. The R1 detail contradicts itself. Sec 5.2.3 says GRPO avoids "extensive critic networks" (and Eq 22 / the "dual-attention critic V_psi" in "Trajectory Pruning" then describe a critic). Eq 22 gives an adaptive entropy coefficient lambda_t = alpha*exp(-beta*Var(R)). A "stepwise reward model f_theta" trained on step-level human CoT labels is described as R1's reward. Yet Fig 13 and the Fig 17 caption show a "Rule-based Reward System". The survey gives no citation for the entropy, dual-attention or stepwise-RM mechanisms, so I could not verify them from the text. Do not cite them without checking the R1 paper.
  2. The claim that R1-Zero reaches "performance comparable to or exceeding models initialized with SFT, such as its DeepSeek-R1 counterpart" (p.31) has no numbers. It also sits oddly with the survey's own Fig 13 label "Drawback" for R1-Zero.
  3. Table 1 parameter sizes are dubious or unsourced. Examples are Claude2 "2B", Claude3.5 "175B", GPT-4 "180B", o1 "300B", GPT-3 "17.5B" (GPT-3 is 175B, as the intro itself says). Do not reuse them.
  4. Quantisation text says "X H (30-bit floating point)". That is almost certainly a typo for 32-bit.
  5. Sec 10 says "senven" open problems but lists eight headings. Sec 11 says alignment origins "in 2018".
  6. Table 2 labels GRPO as "Implicit Reward / AI feedback", which is hard to square with a rule-based reward.
- Dated: the cutoff is about Mar 2025 (R1, o1/o3, Kimi-k1.5, Claude 3.7, Qwen2.5). No DAPO, GSPO, RLVR-at-scale analysis, or INTELLECT/GLM-style systems. Today is 2026-11, so this predates much of the RLVR literature.

BUILDS ON (as printed): PPO Schulman et al. 2017 [46]; InstructGPT Ouyang et al. 2022 [45]; RLHF Bai et al. 2022 (HH-RLHF) [104]; Constitutional AI Bai et al. 2022 [105]; RLAIF Lee et al. 2023/ICML [108,157]; DPO Rafailov et al. 2024 [49]; Bradley-Terry [158]; GRPO via DeepSeekMath Shao et al. 2024 [64]; DeepSeek-R1 DeepSeek-AI 2025 [28]; ReFT Luong et al. 2024 [103]; RLOO [112]; A2C Mnih 2016 [200]; Ziegler et al. 2020 [16] (RLHF summarisation); OpenAI o1 system card Jaech et al. 2024 [41].

CODE: none in the paper (no pseudocode or snippets). Equations worth lifting, with equation numbers: PPO clip (Eq 2), DPO loss (Eq 20), GRPO objective (Eq 8), KL-regularised reward (Eq 13/14).

FIGURES (no captions tool run; names from the extracted text):
- Fig 8 (p.19): RLHF workflow, reward training and policy training. Gives the two-stage picture quickly.
- Fig 9 (p.21): online vs offline RLHF.
- Fig 10 (p.22): RLHF vs RLAIF, differing only in where the reward comes from.
- Fig 11 (p.24): DPO pipeline with frozen reference and trained LM.
- Fig 7 (p.17): ReFT, SFT warm-up then on-policy RL.
- Fig 13 (p.30): R1-Zero (pure RL with a rule-based reward) vs R1 (cold start, two RL stages). This is the most useful figure, but see the LIMITS on its consistency.
- Fig 1/3 (pp.6, 9): timelines of post-training techniques.
- Table 2 (p.18): alignment method comparison grid.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found in the PDF text. Equations are flattened (fractions and subscripts garbled), so I quoted only prose; Eq 2, 8, 20 are described, not quoted. One extraction line, "(30-bit floating point)", may be a source typo rather than an extraction fault. Table 1 and Table 6 contain "[? ]" unresolved citations in the source. I did not run the figures.py captions tool, so the figure captions above are paraphrased from the extraction, not verbatim from the tool.
